source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following
finding: Storing every past run in a memory bank made agents worse than a small fixed, checked memory. Storing only checked runs (strict) made them better. Gap 7: stale or wrong stored items do harm.
numbers: Table 1 (4 agents; success or accuracy; memory size): RegAgent fixed 67.53 (100) vs add-all 55.48 (4100) vs strict 70.95 (2938). EHRAgent fixed 16.75 vs add-all 13.05 vs strict 38.50. AgentDriver fixed 40.11 vs add-all 32.32 vs strict 51.00. CIC-IoT fixed 71.50 vs add-all 59.90 vs strict 85.40. Coarse LLM judges C1/C2/C3 fell between (RegAgent 63.18/65.78/67.35).
quote: the fixed-memory baseline maintains strong results ... sometimes even surpassing runs guided by coarse evaluators
limits: Memory items are past query-execution pairs, not abstract subgoal chunks. Strict evaluator is a ground-truth oracle. Four agents, GPT-4o-mini/4.1-mini class backbones.
agent_relevance: A subgoal library needs a quality gate at write time. Add-all libraries lose to a small verified one. Gate on verified success, not on the model's own judgement.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) experience-following, error propagation, deletion
finding: When a new task is close to a stored item, the agent copies the stored output (output similarity rises with input similarity, Pearson r near 1). So a wrong stored item spreads to later tasks. Deleting items by their later utility helped when the judge was reliable.
numbers: Error-free retrieval variant (same retrieved items, ground-truth outputs) shows an immediate gap for add-all and coarse addition, which widens over the stream. Strict AgentDriver approaches then passes the error-free variant after about 2000 executions. Table 2 with strict judge, history-based deletion: EHRAgent 38.67 to 42.06 (memory 1012 to 784), AgentDriver 51.00 to 51.81, CIC-IoT 85.40 to 89.60. Combined deletion keeps accuracy near (42.34, 49.97, 85.50) with memory about 248, 323, 188.
limits: With a weaker (GPT-4o-mini) deletion judge the effect flips: gain on EHRAgent, loss on AgentDriver. No pure staleness (drift over time) test.
agent_relevance: Library maintenance: delete by downstream utility, only with a trusted judge. Expect copy-the-nearest behaviour: a chunk that matches by surface will be followed even if wrong (links gap 3).

source: Ouyang et al. (2026, ICLR) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Distilled strategy items (from successes and failures) beat no memory and beat routine memories (Synapse, AWM) on WebArena. Total tokens rose only a little, so the gain is not paid for by extra thinking.
numbers: WebArena overall success (684 tasks), Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5, Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8 (steps 9.7 to 8.3). Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7 / 47.7 / 47.6 / 53.9. Claude-3.7-sonnet 41.7 / 42.6 / 40.8 / 46.3. Tokens per task: no memory 50,847; ReasoningBank about +4.3% total tokens for +20.5% relative success. AWM was below no-memory for Claude-3.7 (40.8 vs 41.7).
limits: Authors' own runs; items are text strategies, not executable chunks. Cost study on one backbone. Benchmarks WebArena, Mind2Web, SWE-Bench-Verified.
agent_relevance: Closest to gap 1 (equal tokens): a memory arm can beat no memory at near-equal tokens. No zero-reuse ablation, so reuse vs self-correction is still not separated.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: MaTTS memory vs scaling ablation
finding: Giving the same extra compute to an agent with no memory gave small, unstable gains. With good memory the same extra rollouts gave steady gains. Memory and compute are separable and interact.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash, best-of-5: no memory 39.0 to 42.2; Synapse 44.4; AWM 47.6; ReasoningBank 49.7 to 55.1. Parallel scaling without memory fluctuates 39.0-42.2, sequential 37.4-40.6; with memory parallel 49.7 to 55.1, sequential 49.7 to 54.5.
limits: One subset (187 tasks), one backbone. Best-of-N needs a judge.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: spend extra thinking only when memory exists to steer it. Gap 1: compute-matched view exists (no-memory at 5 rollouts 42.2 vs memory at 1 rollout 49.7).

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank appendix C.1: number of retrieved items
finding: More retrieved memory items lowered success. One item was best.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 39.0; 1 item 49.7; 2 items 46.5; 3 items 45.5; 4 items 44.4.
quote: the relevance and quality of memory are more crucial than sheer quantity
limits: One backbone, one subset. Authors explain it as conflicts or noise between items.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a bigger active set hurts even when every item is relevant. Fits a small working set; retrieve few, not many.

source: Lei et al. (2026) SkillEvolBench: from episodic experience to procedural skills
finding: Across 10 model configurations and 3 agent harnesses, distilled skills were unstable on frozen deployment tasks and often lost to replaying raw trajectories. A static curated skill set did worse than no skills on average.
numbers: 180 tasks, 6 environments. Raw-Trajectory is the strongest baseline by mean RSR 48.2, ESR 37.6, ARSR 44.7, CompSR 25.7 (%). Curated-Static: improves 2 models, ties 1, hurts 7; mean ESR change -2.44 points. Claude Opus 4.6 self-generated: +5.5 LSR and +10.0 RSR but lower ESR, CSSR, CompSR.
quote: Raw-trajectory reuse frequently outperforms distilled skills
limits: Authors' own benchmark; no confidence intervals in the text read. Skills are written instructions, not code chunks.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 7: a chunk library is not free. Keep the concrete trace next to the abstraction; use raw-trace reuse as a control arm.

source: Lei et al. (2026) SkillEvolBench capacity diagnostic (Tier-3 libraries)
finding: Forcing agents to write bigger skill libraries with extra resource files cut frozen-task success for some models. Bigger was not better.
numbers: ESR: Gemini 3 Flash 35.6% (no skill) to 27.8% (SelfGen-Always+Tier3); Claude Sonnet 4.5 35.6% to 30.0%. GPT-5.4 best ESR with Curated-Always; the larger +Tier3 libraries reduced ESR. Gap between easiest and hardest environment: 67.3 points LSR, 42.1 points ESR, versus 1.9 and 5.4 across baselines.
quote: larger and more expensive libraries can fail when capacity expansion is not matched
limits: Authors' causes (stale context, over-specific validators, weak triggers) come from trace reading, not from a test.
agent_relevance: Direct measured harm from large or cluttered libraries (gap 7). Cap library size and prune; domain matters more than method.

source: Yu et al. (2026) SkillLens: adaptive multi-granularity skill reuse
finding: Skills kept at four levels (policy, strategy, procedure, primitive) and reused at mixed level beat flat single-level libraries, and used far fewer evolution tokens than rewriting whole skills.
numbers: ALFWorld success: baseline 45.00; AutoSkill 47.14; EvoSkill 47.14; SkillLens 51.31. MuLocbench bug localisation Acc@1 up to +6.31 points over the best skill baseline. Evolution cost: 16.41M tokens vs 115.51M for the rewrite-all variant; cost rises 22.7% when the skill ratio goes from 25% to 100%.
limits: Two benchmarks, authors' own baselines, gains of 4 to 6 points, no variance in the text read. Not a clean single-granularity sweep.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no single best chunk size; keep a hierarchy and choose the level at retrieval. Store subgoals at more than one grain.

source: Yu et al. (2026) Skill is Not One-Size-Fits-All (MASA): skill granularity by model size
finding: With content fixed, the best skill length depended on the model. For one model every skill length hurt.
numbers: ALFWorld, Qwen3 4B/8B/14B/32B, levels Concise (~370 tokens), Moderate (~1,092), Detailed (~2,737). Qwen3-4B best with Moderate; 14B and 32B best with Detailed; Qwen3-8B best with no skill (32.1%) and all three skill levels lowered it. MASA reports gains up to 25.8 points over the strongest baseline.
limits: Qwen3 family only; granularity here is text length, not chunk structure.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 8: skill size must be tuned per backbone. Test our library at 2 to 3 sizes on the model we use; a skill can override a model's own short, correct plan.

source: He et al. (2026) Beyond Domains: SkillMigrator, transferable interaction patterns
finding: Skill retrieval by instruction wording alone misses skills when page structure is the same but wording changes. Adding a layout-structure signal restored reuse. Without it the gain over no skills vanished.
numbers: 60-task Mind2Web subset, GPT-4.1: reuse of ASI, SkillWeaver, PolySkill falls from cross-task to cross-website to cross-domain. Ablation: removing the layout signal drops WebArena SR 45.7 to 39.2 (no-skill baseline 38.5). Mind2Web cross-domain 59.4 to 55.8 without layout; no synonym pool 57.0. Cross-domain reuse 35.4% vs PolySkill 31%. LLM-action count down 8 to 10% at matched success. Claude-4 gives 54.7% vs GPT-4.1 45.7% on WebArena.
limits: Authors' own system and ablations; not a paraphrase test as such.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 9: a library keyed only by task wording fails under surface change. Key chunks by structure (state shape) plus text. Mirrors human location and format specificity.

source: He et al. (2026) Beyond Domains: slot-filled templates across sites
finding: Each stored skill is a template with slots bound to live page elements at use time; reusing a template across sites is what makes it cross-domain. No paper I opened ran static-vs-slot with everything else equal.
numbers: Mind2Web, GPT-4.1, ReAct (no skill) SR 53.8 / 56.2 / 62.3 (cross-task / cross-website / cross-domain). The per-method static rows were garbled in text extraction and are not quoted.
limits: Slot templates are compared with other skill libraries, not with fixed unparametrised chunks in a clean ablation.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. The Gobet-Simon template idea is used in practice but the controlled slots-vs-no-slots contrast is not measured for LLMs.

source: Hu et al. (2026) SELM: self-evolving skill library management
finding: Library growth alone did not help. Gating changes by validation and pruning skills with negative feedback mattered most.
numbers: SpreadsheetBench, Claude-Opus-4.6, no harness: full 56.5; no validation gate 42.5; no utility score 46.3; no utility-aware retrieval 49.2; no graveyard 50.4; no meta skill 53.1; no meta skill + slow update 42.7. Qwen3-30B-A3B: 5 initial skills 17.5%; epoch 1 adds 5 skills and accuracy stays 17.5; epoch 2 adds 2, downvotes 4, accuracy 30.0; final held-out 36.43.
limits: One benchmark for the ablation. Text says 36.43% is compared with a 30.0% no-skill baseline, but 30.0 is also the epoch-2 selection figure, so the baseline value is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: add a validation gate, utility scores and a graveyard. Adding skills without feedback gave no gain at epoch 1.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization using chess (v3 full text)
finding: GPT-5 at moderate effort chose by itself to think much longer on unfamiliar positions, yet gained less per token. This clarifies the earlier unclear per-token figure.
numbers: Reasoning tokens (moderate effort): 3,426 (SD 1,967) well-known, 11,800 (SD 5,606) near, 16,953 (SD 6,832) random. Relative ACPL gain per 1,000 tokens: 22.55% well-known, 7.23% near (-67.98%), 3.81% random (-83.10%). Total ACPL drop with reasoning 71.74% (WD 77.25, ND 85.3, OOD 64.69). Moderate-effort ACPL: WD 11.72, OOD 298.81; OOD/WD ratio widens from 16x to 25x.
limits: v3 text gives -67.98% and -83.10%; the earlier critique quoted about -50% and -89% (older version or abstract). Use v3 and flag the version.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answered in direction: token use rises as library hit falls, but return per token falls. Cap thinking on unfamiliar tasks; spend on search for new chunks only with a stopping rule.

source: Pleiss et al. (2026) cross-lineage check: Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3 Flash
finding: The same familiarity gradient appeared for Claude and Gemini. This is the authors' own extension, not an independent replication, and chess only.
numbers: Minimal reasoning. Claude Opus 4.6 ACPL: WD 14.0, ND 207.2, OOD 728.6; illegal moves 0.2%, 8.2%, 51.6%. Gemini 3 Flash ACPL: WD 34.8, ND 434.1, OOD 829.7; illegal 2.2%, 17.0%, 72.0%. Syntactically invalid output: Claude 14.4% of positions, Gemini 0.047%. GPT-5 OOD illegal moves 33.8%.
limits: Different data collection windows; authors warn against ranking lineages. Same team. No non-chess domain.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: replication across 3 model families by the same authors only. Independent and non-chess replication not found.

source: Gong et al. (2023) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study (n-back)
finding: ChatGPT shows a human-like capacity limit in verbal and spatial n-back tasks. This is a span-style test, not a chunked-vs-unchunked test.
numbers: Abstract only: no numeric results on the page (AAAI-24).
limits: Only the abstract page was read. It does not test chunking or the Chase-Simon meaningful-vs-random contrast.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: nearest LLM span study I could open; the chunking contrast is still untested.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks (ASI)
finding: Skills stored as verified programs beat the static agent and beat the text-skill version, mainly because induced programs are checked.
numbers: WebArena: +23.5% over static baseline agent, +11.3% over text-skill counterpart; 10.7% to 15.3% fewer steps.
limits: Abstract page only; relative gains; full ablation not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: executable plus verified beats text-only here, while MASA says fit to the model matters. Vary both axes on our agent.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) SkillWeaver: web agents self-improve by discovering and honing skills
finding: Skills written as APIs by a strong agent also helped weaker agents.
numbers: Relative success gains 31.8% and 39.8% on WebArena and real sites; up to 54.3% on WebArena for weaker agents using stronger agents' APIs.
limits: Abstract page only. Transfer here is across agents, not across domains. Author list not read, so first-author attribution is unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: libraries can move between models; domain-boundness is still not measured.
